chapter_title: Kotlin Fundamentals - Control Flow and Functions

screens.title: Control Flow and Functions in Kotlin
screens.subtitle: Decisions, repetition, and reusable code for readable Android logic

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how Kotlin lets your program make decisions, repeat work, and package functionality into named routines. You will see that Kotlin treats conditionals like expressions that can return values, giving you concise ways to assign results directly. You will also learn loop forms to traverse ranges and collections reliably, and how break and continue change loop execution. Finally, we will organize behavior into functions: named units with parameters, return types, defaults, and convenient single-expression forms. A concrete example you will use throughout is a small calculator program that uses a while loop to accept operations, a when expression to dispatch arithmetic, and functions for each operation including a safe divide that returns null on division by zero. Why this matters: these tools let you build responsive, maintainable Android code instead of long linear scripts. As you explore, pay attention to common pitfalls: infinite loops, non-exhaustive when expressions, and forgetting explicit return types when they clarify intent. By the end you will be able to combine these features in a simple interactive program and reason about correctness.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Control flow (if/when, loops) plus functions let you write compact, safe, and reusable Kotlin code for Android behavior.

narration.text: By the end of these lessons you will implement conditionals and expressions, control iteration, and define reusable functions in Kotlin. First, you will use if-else chains and the when expression to make choices and return values directly from conditionals. This matters because expression-style conditionals reduce boilerplate and make assignments concise. Second, you will iterate with for, while, and do-while loops, using ranges, until, downTo, and step to control sequence and direction. You will practice preventing infinite loops and using break and continue carefully. Third, you will define functions with typed parameters and return types, including Unit, and you will reason about when to declare return types explicitly. Fourth, you will apply single-expression functions, default arguments, and named arguments to write shorter, clearer function calls. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a verification milestone so you can check your competency by building the example calculator program that combines loops, when, and arithmetic functions.

screens.title: The if Expression
screens.subtitle: Use if as an expression that returns a value

narration.text: Kotlin treats if not only as a control statement but as an expression that evaluates to a value. That means you can assign the result of conditional logic directly to a variable, eliminating extra temporary variables and making intent clearer. For example, a common pattern is to pick the maximum of two numbers with val max = if (a > b) a else b; the if returns either a or b. When branches contain blocks, each branch must return a compatible type so the expression has a single resulting type. A concrete example: when choosing a weather message you can write val weatherMessage = if (temperature > 30) "It's hot outside!" else if (temperature > 20) "Pleasant weather." else "It's a bit chilly.". A common misconception is thinking if expressions require an else; they do not when used as statements, but when used as expressions that must produce a value on every path, you must provide all possible branches or the compiler will report an error. Key takeaway: prefer expression-style if when you need a value and ensure branch types align. How would you rewrite a short chain into a single-expression assignment in your code?

keyIdea.title: If as value
keyIdea.text: Use if to compute and assign a value directly, keeping branches type-compatible and exhaustive when required.

content.html:
Definition
if as an expression
An if expression evaluates conditions and returns the chosen branch value. Branches must yield compatible types when assigned.
Explanation
  • An if can return a value directly to a variable.
  • Use else to ensure an expression returns a value on every path.
  • If branches include blocks, the last expression in the block is the branch value.
Example
val a = 7
val b = 5
val max = if (a > b) a else b
println("Max: $max") // Prints Max: 7
Key Takeaway

Use if expressions to compute values concisely; ensure each branch produces a compatible type and include else when needed.

Common Pitfall
Omitting an else when the expression needs a value causes a compile-time error. Another mistake is mixing incompatible branch types.
Analogy
Think of an if expression as asking a question that hands back an answer you can store; the answer must be the same kind no matter which path answers.
Try this
Rewrite a piece of code that sets a status string using nested if-else statements into a single assignment using an if expression. Confirm the branch types match.

screens.title: The when Expression
screens.subtitle: Versatile pattern matching that returns values

narration.text: The when expression replaces the traditional switch and gives you powerful pattern matching. It can match single values, multiple comma-separated values, ranges, or even type checks and arbitrary boolean conditions. When used as an expression, when must be exhaustive: every possible input must be handled or you must provide an else branch. For example, mapping a numeric day to a label can be written as: when (dayOfWeek) { 1, 7 -> "Weekend"; in 2..6 -> "Weekday"; else -> "Invalid day" }. You can return the result of when directly to a variable, which simplifies branching logic. A misconception is assuming when only works with constants; in fact you can use complex conditions and type checks like when (obj) { is String ->... }. Another important point is that when used without an argument it evaluates boolean expressions in each branch, making it like a concise chain of if-else checks. The key takeaway is to use when when you have multiple distinct cases to match and make it exhaustive to let the compiler help you catch unhandled inputs. The when Expression means use when for multi-way branching, matching values, ranges, types, and boolean conditions; make it exhaustive when used as an expression.. In practical terms, versatile pattern matching that returns values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: When power
keyIdea.text: Use when for multi-way branching, matching values, ranges, types, and boolean conditions; make it exhaustive when used as an expression.

content.html:
Definition
when expression
A versatile multi-branch expression that can match values, ranges, and types, and can return a value when exhaustive.
Example
val dayOfWeek = 3
val dayType = when (dayOfWeek) {
  1, 7 -> "Weekend"
  in 2..6 -> "Weekday"
  else -> "Invalid day"
}
println(dayType) // Prints "Weekday"
Variants
  • when with argument: matches the value against branches.
  • when without argument: evaluates boolean expressions in each branch.
  • use is for type checks inside when branches.
Common Misconception
Thinking when is limited to constants. It can handle ranges and type checks and even arbitrary conditions when used without an argument.
Concrete Scenario
Detect an object's runtime type and print its detail: when (obj) { is String -> println("Length ${obj.length}") is Int -> println("Value $obj") else -> println("Unknown") }.
Key Takeaway

Use when for clear multi-case logic and prefer exhaustiveness for safety; use else to cover unknown inputs.

screens.title: Type Checks and when Variants
screens.subtitle: Use is checks and boolean branches in when expressions

narration.text: Kotlin's when supports runtime type checks with the is operator and boolean branches when used without a subject. This flexibility means you can write compact, readable dispatch logic. For example, given val obj: Any = "Hello" you can use when (obj) { is String -> println("It's a String of length ${obj. length}") is Int -> println("It's an Int with value $obj") else -> println("Unknown type") }. When used without an argument, each branch is a boolean expression, like when { x % 2 == 0 -> "even" x % 2 == 1 -> "odd" else -> "unknown" }. A common mistake is to assume that is branches require casting; Kotlin smart casts the variable inside the branch when the check succeeds, so you can access String properties directly. Another pitfall is non-exhaustive when when used as an expression — always include else or cover all sealed or enum cases. Practice creating a when that handles String, Int, and other types and observe how smart casting simplifies subsequent code. Would you prefer when or if chains for your use case and why?

keyIdea.title: Type-aware branching
keyIdea.text: Use is for type checks and rely on smart casts; use when without subject for boolean-style branches.

content.html:
Process Flow
when with type checks
Smart casts let you use the checked type inside the branch without explicit casts.
val obj: Any = "Hello"
when (obj) {
  is String -> println("It's a String of length ${obj.length}")
  is Int -> println("It's an Int with value $obj")
  else -> println("Unknown type")
}
Why this helps
  • Reduces boilerplate casting code.
  • Combines type checks with handling logic in one place.
  • When without subject supports complex boolean conditions per branch.
Example
when without subject
val x = 5
val parity = when {
  x % 2 == 0 -> "even"
  x % 2 == 1 -> "odd"
  else -> "unknown"
}
Misconception
Assuming smart cast works outside branches. Smart casts apply only where the compiler can prove the type after the check.

screens.title: for Loop and Ranges
screens.subtitle: Iterate ranges, collections, and control step and direction

narration.text: Kotlin's for loop is simple and expressive for iterating ranges, arrays, and collections. Use for (i in 1..5) for an inclusive range from 1 to 5, and for (i in 1 until 5) to iterate from 1 up to but excluding 5. You can iterate backward with downTo and control stepping with step. For example, for (i in 10 downTo 0 step 2) prints 10, 8, 6, and so on. When iterating collections, you iterate elements directly: for (item in list) {... }. A useful pattern is for ((index, value) in list. withIndex()) to access positions. A common misunderstanding is assuming until includes the end; it does not. Also avoid modifying the collection you're iterating over unless using appropriate iterators to avoid concurrent modification issues. For Android code, use these loops to populate UI lists or run short background computations, but prefer higher-level collection APIs like map and forEach when you need transformations. Can you pick a case where step and downTo make the loop clearer than a manual index calculation? for Loop and Ranges means use .. for inclusive ranges, until to exclude the end, downto to go backwards and step to control increments.. In practical terms, iterate ranges, collections, and control step and direction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Range iteration
keyIdea.text: Use .. for inclusive ranges, until to exclude the end, downTo to go backwards and step to control increments.

content.html:
Comparison
for with ranges vs collections
Ranges are numeric sequences; collections iterate elements directly. Choose the form that communicates intent.
// Inclusive range
for (i in 1..5) println(i) // 1,2,3,4,5

// Exclusive end
for (i in 1 until 5) println(i) // 1,2,3,4

// Backwards with step
for (i in 10 downTo 0 step 2) println(i) // 10,8,6,4,2,0
Best Practices
  • Prefer for-each over manual indices for collections when you only need values.
  • Use withIndex when you need the index.
  • Remember until excludes the upper bound; use .. when inclusive behavior is required.
Key Takeaway

Use range helpers to express sequence direction and step clearly instead of manually adjusting indices.

screens.title: while vs do-while
screens.subtitle: Pre-check and post-check loop behavior and hazards

narration.text: While and do-while loops control repetition with different checking points. A while loop checks its condition before every iteration, so the loop body may not run at all if the condition is false initially. In contrast, a do-while loop executes its body first and checks the condition after, guaranteeing at least one execution. For example, a do-while can be useful when you need to prompt a user and then repeat based on their response. One major pitfall with while loops is accidentally creating an infinite loop by failing to update the condition variable. Always ensure the loop body moves the state toward termination. A good habit is to reason about the loop invariant and prove that each iteration reduces the distance to the stop condition. Another common mistake is misplacing continues or breaks when multiple nested loops exist; break and continue affect only the innermost loop. The takeaway: choose while when the condition must hold before running, and do-while when the body must run at least once. Ask yourself: can you show the loop variable moves toward termination on each iteration?

keyIdea.title: Loop checks
keyIdea.text: Use while for pre-checked loops and do-while when the body must run once; always design loops to terminate.

content.html:
Definition
while and do-while
A while checks before each iteration; a do-while checks after, guaranteeing one execution.
// While example
var x = 0
while (x < 3) {
  println("While loop: $x")
  x++
}

// Do-while example
var y = 0
do {
  println("Do-While loop: $y")
  y++
} while (y < 0) // executes once
Common Mistake
Infinite loops from failing to update the loop variable are frequent. Check that each iteration progresses state toward the stopping condition.
Guided Check
  • Identify the loop variable and its range.
  • Confirm the body updates that variable toward the end condition.
  • Consider edge cases where the condition is initially false or true indefinitely.

narration.text: Break and continue let you change the loop flow without restructuring the loop. break exits the innermost loop immediately, moving execution to the statement after that loop. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and proceeds to the next iteration by re-evaluating the loop condition. Use continue when you need to ignore certain values without nesting additional conditionals. For example, in a for loop over 1..5, if i equals 3 you might continue to skip printing three, and break when you reach a termination value. Overuse of break and continue can make loops harder to read, so prefer clear loop conditions or early returns in functions when possible. A common trap is assuming break exits outer loops; it only exits the innermost loop. When you need to exit multiple loops, consider refactoring into a function and using return, or using labeled breaks carefully. The takeaway: use break and continue for local control, but keep their usage minimal to preserve readability. break and continue means use break to exit and continue to skip to the next iteration; labels can change scope but use them sparingly.. In practical terms, fine-grained control inside loops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Loop modifiers
keyIdea.text: Use break to exit and continue to skip to the next iteration; labels can change scope but use them sparingly.

content.html:
Definition
break and continue behavior
Use break to stop a loop and continue to skip the current iteration.
for (i in 1..5) {
  if (i == 3) continue // skip 3
  if (i == 5) break    // stop loop at 5
  println("Loop value: $i") // Prints 1, 2, 4
}
When to avoid them
  • Avoid deep nesting with many breaks; it reduces clarity.
  • Consider extracting logic into functions and using return instead of labeled breaks.
Pro Tip
If you need to break out of multiple nested loops, refactor into a helper function and use return to exit early instead of complex labels.
Key Takeaway

Use break and continue for local loop control, but prefer simple loop conditions and small helper functions for complex flow.

screens.title: Functions: Signature and Return Types
screens.subtitle: Define behavior with fun, parameters, and explicit returns

narration.text: Functions package behavior into named units with clear signatures. In Kotlin you define functions with the fun keyword followed by a name, parameters with types, and an optional return type. If a function returns meaningful data you should declare its return type explicitly to make the contract clear; functions that return no meaningful value use Unit and can omit it. Example: fun calculateSum(a: Int, b: Int): Int { return a + b } clearly shows inputs and output. Another common pattern is a greet function that returns a formatted string. A frequent mistake is forgetting to set a return type when using explicit return statements, which can cause confusing compiler feedback. Functions promote modularity, testability, and reuse — for Android, extracting logic into functions keeps Activities and Fragments focused on UI coordination instead of raw computation. Practice by writing small arithmetic functions with explicit return types to confirm the compiler enforces the expected behavior. How would you design function signatures to make data flow explicit in your app? Functions: Signature and Return Types means declare parameters and return types to document behavior; use unit for no meaningful return and prefer explicit types when helpful.. In practical terms, define behavior with fun, parameters, and explicit returns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Function contracts
keyIdea.text: Declare parameters and return types to document behavior; use Unit for no meaningful return and prefer explicit types when helpful.

content.html:
Definition
Function signature and return
Define inputs and outputs clearly so callers know what to pass and expect back.
fun calculateSum(a: Int, b: Int): Int {
  return a + b
}

fun printMessage(message: String) { // returns Unit
  println(message)
}
Common Pitfall
Not declaring a return type for non-Unit functions makes intent unclear. Prefer explicit types for public APIs and library code.
Key Takeaway

Write clear function signatures. When in doubt, state the return type to document behavior and help the compiler catch mistakes.

screens.title: Single-expression Functions
screens.subtitle: Concise function bodies with equals syntax

narration.text: Single-expression functions let you write compact, readable code for simple operations. Instead of a block with return, use an equals sign and an expression: fun multiply(a: Int, b: Int) = a * b. The compiler infers the return type, which keeps short utility functions terse. This form is ideal for pure functions that compute and return a single value. However, a misconception is assuming single-expression forms are appropriate for complex logic; prefer full blocks when multiple statements, local variables, or early returns are needed. Another caution is that type inference can hide mistakes in public APIs; for library or shared code consider declaring the return type explicitly even for single-expression functions. Example: fun subtract(a: Int, b: Int) = a - b demonstrates the compact form. Use single-expression functions to reduce ceremony in helpers and keep the code readable, but balance terseness with clarity for your team. Single-expression Functions means use single-expression functions for simple returns; prefer explicit types for public or complex functions.. In practical terms, concise function bodies with equals syntax. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Concise functions
keyIdea.text: Use single-expression functions for simple returns; prefer explicit types for public or complex functions.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Single-expression examples
Short functions can be written with equals and no braces for clarity.
fun subtract(a: Int, b: Int) = a - b
fun multiply(a: Int, b: Int) = a * b

println("Difference: ${subtract(10, 4)}") // Difference: 6
When to expand
If you need multiple statements, exception handling, or early returns, prefer a full function body for clarity and debuggability.
Key Takeaway

Prefer single-expression functions for trivial transforms; expand to blocks when logic grows or explicit types are helpful.

screens.title: Default and Named Arguments
screens.subtitle: Reduce overloads and improve call-site clarity

narration.text: Default arguments let you supply default values for parameters in function definitions so callers can omit them. This pattern reduces the need for multiple overloaded functions. Named arguments let callers specify parameters by name, improving readability and allowing arguments to be passed in any order. For example, fun sendMessage(message: String, recipient: String = "User", priority: Int = 1) lets you call sendMessage("Welcome") to use defaults or sendMessage("Feedback", priority = 5) using the default recipient. Named arguments are especially useful when functions have many parameters with defaults; you can override only those you need and make the call self-documenting. A common misuse is overloading defaults in ways that create ambiguous calls; keep signatures clear and prefer small numbers of parameters or data classes for grouped options. The takeaway: use defaults and named arguments to simplify APIs and make call sites easier to read and maintain. Default and Named Arguments means use default and named arguments to reduce overloads and make call sites explicit and flexible.. In practical terms, reduce overloads and improve call-site clarity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Flexible calls
keyIdea.text: Use default and named arguments to reduce overloads and make call sites explicit and flexible.

content.html:
Definition
Default and named args
Provide defaults in the signature and use named args to skip or reorder parameters at call sites.
fun sendMessage(
  message: String,
  recipient: String = "User",
  priority: Int = 1
) {
  println("Sending '$message' to $recipient with priority $priority")
}

sendMessage("Welcome")
sendMessage("Urgent update!", "Admin")
sendMessage(message = "Reminder", priority = 3)
Best Practice
Use named arguments for clarity when skipping defaults. Favor small parameter lists or option objects for many settings.
Key Takeaway

Defaults and named arguments simplify calls and document intent. Use them thoughtfully to keep APIs readable and unambiguous.

screens.title: Calculator Example: Integrating Loops, when, and Functions
screens.subtitle: Walkthrough of the starter calculator program

narration.text: Let's walk through the provided calculator starter that combines loops, when, and functions. The program defines arithmetic functions — add, subtract, multiply, and a divide that returns null on division by zero — demonstrating typed return values and null safety. The main loop uses a while to repeatedly prompt for input until the user opts out. Inside the loop, a when expression dispatches the chosen operation to the appropriate function. If divide returns null, the code prints an error about division by zero. After each calculation the program asks whether to continue; any answer other than yes breaks the loop. This example shows how small functions keep the main loop focused on control flow and input and output while business logic stays testable. A misconception is placing heavy logic inside the loop; extract calculations into functions to ease testing and readability. Try extending the divide function to return an explanatory error type or message instead of null to see how return types affect caller handling. What small helper would you extract next to make the main loop even clearer? Calculator Example: Integrating Loops, when, and Functions means split i/o and control flow from computation using functions; use when for dispatch and while for the interactive main loop.. In practical terms, walkthrough of the starter calculator program. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Integration
keyIdea.text: Split I/O and control flow from computation using functions; use when for dispatch and while for the interactive main loop.

content.html:
Starter Code Walkthrough
import java.util.Scanner

fun divide(a: Double, b: Double): Double? {
  if (b == 0.0) return null
  return a / b
}

fun main() {
  val reader = Scanner(System.`in`)
  var continueCalculating = true

  while (continueCalculating) {
    // read numbers and operation
    val result: Double? = when (operation) {
      "+" -> add(num1, num2)
      "-" -> subtract(num1, num2)
      "*" -> multiply(num1, num2)
      "/" -> divide(num1, num2)
      else -> null
    }

    // handle null result from divide
  }
}
Concrete Example
If the user enters division by zero, divide returns null and the main loop prints an error message instead of a numeric result, demonstrating safe handling of exceptional conditions without exceptions.
Check
Refactor: extract input parsing into a helper function and observe how the main loop becomes a clear orchestrator of prompts and calls.

narration.text: Let's summarize the core concepts you should retain. First, if in Kotlin can be an expression that returns a value; use it to compute assignments concisely and ensure branches produce compatible types. Second, when is a versatile multi-way expression that matches values, ranges, types, or boolean conditions; make it exhaustive or provide an else branch when used as an expression. Third, for, while, and do-while let you iterate in different scenarios: use ranges and step for numeric sequences, while for pre-checked loops, and do-while when a single guaranteed execution is needed. Each of these concepts helps you write clearer, safer control flow. In practice, combine them with small functions to keep UI code compact and testable. Which concept will you apply first in your project? Key Concepts means if and when are expressions; loops have clear checking semantics; combine with functions for clean code.. In practical terms, what to remember. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: If and when are expressions; loops have clear checking semantics; combine with functions for clean code.

narration.text: Finish with the most actionable reminders. Functions are defined with fun and should declare parameters and return types to document behavior; Unit indicates no meaningful return. Single-expression functions shorten simple computations but prefer explicit return types for public APIs. Default and named arguments simplify calls and reduce overloads, improving call-site readability. Watch for common mistakes: non-exhaustive when expressions used as values, infinite loops from missing updates, and accidentally mixing incompatible types in conditional branches. In your projects, prefer small functions with clear contracts and choose the loop or conditional form that best communicates intent.
